1	\paragraph{Conclusion.}
2	We analyzed three VLA architectures (OpenVLA, TracVLA, NORA) across four LIBERO task suites, comparing trained and reference checkpoints to decompose VLA fine-tuning into training-associated and inherited representational effects.
3	Two training-associated effects are consistent across two VLM-to-VLA transitions: $R^2$ exit collapse, where action-relevant information encoded at intermediate layers is selectively less decodable at exit layers (6/6 cells, sign test $p = 0.016$), and counterfactual sensitivity, where all trained models respond to instruction perturbation (Cohen's $d \geq 0.45$ across eight tested cells).
4	Exit collapse is consistently observed across all tested VLM-to-VLA conditions (6/6 cells, $\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.455$), but does not re-emerge in VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning (0/4 standard cells, $\Delta R^2 = 0.033$--$0.086$); an NLP finetuning control on the same backbone ($\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) is consistent with this effect being specific to action-oriented training.
5	In contrast, L1 instruction-dominant attention is inherited from base-model pretraining: one backbone (Phi-3-Vision) saturates at 32/32 heads before any action training.
6	Metric incomparability between trained (action MSE) and reference (cosine distance) conditions precludes quantifying counterfactual amplification factors.
7	Extending this framework to flow-matching and diffusion VLAs with cross-attention, to benchmarks with richer language grounding, and to intermediate training checkpoints are priorities for future work.
8	Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

114	\paragraph{Metric constraints on trained--reference comparison.}
115	Trained models produce action outputs, enabling Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TracVLA) or cosine distance on action tokens (NORA).
116	Reference VLMs (Phi-3-Vision, Qwen2.5-VL) do not generate actions; their sensitivity is measured via cosine distance on hidden representations—a metric with different scale, units, and distributional properties.
117	Ratios between Cohen's $d$ and cosine distance are therefore methodologically invalid, and we do not report cross-metric amplification factors.
118	Qualitatively, reference VLMs show weak sensitivity: the TracVLA reference (Phi-3-Vision) produces peak cosine distances of $0.15$--$0.19$; the NORA reference (Qwen2.5-VL) yields $0.081$ on Goal.

1003	\paragraph{Convergent reorganization from divergent starting points.}
1004	Reference profiles differ qualitatively: OpenVLA (Llama-2) peaks at L0 ($R^2 = 0.629$) then collapses to near-zero at mid-layers (L20: $0.086$, std $= 0.311$), while Phi-3-V peaks at L6 ($0.578 \pm 0.018$) with gradual monotonic decline (late-layer std $= 0.068$).
1005	After VLA training, both architectures reach nearly identical mid-layer peaks—OpenVLA at L9 ($R^2 = 0.637 \pm 0.008$), TraceVLA at L11 ($0.634 \pm 0.009$)—with $\Delta = 0.003$ and overlapping CIs.
1006	Deep-layer variance drops sharply with training: OpenVLA std $0.277 \to 0.040$; Phi-3-V std $0.068 \to 0.011$.
1007	Peak $R^2$ values are comparable before and after training (reference peaks reach $91$--$99\%$ of trained), but peak locations shift deeper (L0$\to$L9; L6$\to$L11) and profile shapes transform from architecture-specific patterns to a shared mid-layer plateau.

1119	Task-specific fine-tuning eliminates L31 re-engagement (18 $\to$ 0 heads; \S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}), consistent with exit-layer attention serving multi-task flexibility ($N{=}2$).
1120	TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} (Phi-3-V) shows consistent entry-exit attention concentration from an opposite starting point (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).
1121	The $2 {\times} 2$ trained-vs-reference comparison reveals a consistent reorganization pattern: reference OpenVLA collapses from L0 ($R^2 = 0.629$) to near-zero at mid-layers (L20: $0.086$, std $= 0.277$), while reference Phi-3-V peaks at L6 ($0.578$) with gradual decline (std $= 0.068$)—qualitatively opposite reference landscapes.
1122	Yet training drives both to nearly identical mid-layer peaks ($0.637$ vs.\ $0.634$, $\Delta = 0.003$) with stabilized deep-layer variance (OpenVLA std $0.277 \to 0.040$; Phi-3-V $0.068 \to 0.011$).
1123	This consistent outcome from divergent starting points suggests that mid-layer action specialization is a consistent convergence pattern of VLA training, not an architectural artifact.

\paragraph{Design implications for VLA training.}
Three patterns in the data motivate design considerations.
First, VLM-to-VLA transitions produce substantial exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.15$--$0.45$) while VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning does not ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$), suggesting that multi-stage training pipelines---where a general-purpose action-capable checkpoint precedes task-specific fine-tuning---may preserve exit-layer action structure that single-stage VLM-to-VLA training loses.
Second, mid-layer action probes consistently outperform exit-layer probes in architectures with pronounced collapse, motivating investigation of early-exit decoding strategies that read actions from intermediate layers rather than the final output.
Third, L1 instruction-dominant attention fractions provide a low-cost signal ($<$1 forward pass) for verifying that instruction routing is intact after fine-tuning; a drop from the reference baseline may indicate degraded instruction processing.
These implications are directional---validating them requires controlled training-stage experiments that the present observational design does not provide.

\paragraph{Behavioral relevance.}
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with published LIBERO success rates across all nine available architecture-suite cells yields a positive but non-significant trend (Spearman $\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$).
Within-suite comparisons, which control for task difficulty, are uniformly positive: on Goal ($n = 3$ architectures), $\Delta R^2$ and success rate are perfectly rank-correlated ($\rho = 1.0$), and every remaining suite ($n = 2$ each) shows the same direction.
This directional evidence is consistent with stronger mid-network action encoding followed by exit-layer compression being associated with better task performance, though architecture capacity differences and limited sample size preclude causal interpretation (extended analysis in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Design implications for VLA training.}
Three patterns in the data motivate design considerations.
First, VLM-to-VLA transitions produce substantial exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.15$--$0.45$) while VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning does not ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$), suggesting that multi-stage training pipelines---where a general-purpose action-capable checkpoint precedes task-specific fine-tuning---may preserve exit-layer action structure that single-stage VLM-to-VLA training loses.
Second, mid-layer action probes consistently outperform exit-layer probes in architectures with pronounced collapse, motivating investigation of early-exit decoding strategies that read actions from intermediate layers rather than the final output.
Third, L1 instruction-dominant attention fractions provide a low-cost signal ($<$1 forward pass) for verifying that instruction routing is intact after fine-tuning; a drop from the reference baseline may indicate degraded instruction processing.
These implications are directional---validating them requires controlled training-stage experiments that the present observational design does not provide.

\paragraph{Behavioral relevance.}
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with published LIBERO success rates across all nine available architecture-suite cells yields a positive but non-significant trend (Spearman $\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$).
Within-suite comparisons, which control for task difficulty, are uniformly positive: on Goal ($n = 3$ architectures), $\Delta R^2$ and success rate are perfectly rank-correlated ($\rho = 1.0$), and every remaining suite ($n = 2$ each) shows the same direction.
This directional evidence is consistent with stronger mid-network action encoding followed by exit-layer compression being associated with better task performance, though architecture capacity differences and limited sample size preclude causal interpretation (extended analysis in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Scope of claims.}
Our analyses are observational---we compare trained and reference checkpoints without intervening on training.
All findings are correlational; we cannot distinguish whether exit collapse is caused by action fine-tuning or by confounded factors (e.g., data distribution, optimization trajectory).
The cross-architecture design ($N = 2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions) strengthens external validity but remains insufficient for strong causal claims.
A systematic claim--evidence--scope summary is provided in Figure~\ref{fig:claim_evidence} (Appendix).

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The $\Delta R^2$ threshold offers a practical diagnostic: computing per-layer action probes requires approximately one GPU-hour and no task-specific labels beyond the training data already available.
A substantial drop ($\Delta R^2 > 0.10$) signals VLM-to-VLA representational reorganization; a flat profile ($< 0.10$) suggests pre-existing action-decoding structure.
This pattern also motivates multi-stage training pipelines---where a general-purpose action-capable checkpoint precedes task-specific fine-tuning---as a strategy that may preserve exit-layer action structure that single-stage VLM-to-VLA training loses.
Additionally, mid-layer probes consistently outperform exit-layer probes in architectures with pronounced collapse, motivating early-exit decoding strategies, and L1 instruction-dominant attention fractions provide a low-cost signal for verifying instruction routing after fine-tuning.
These implications are directional; validating them requires controlled training-stage experiments.

\paragraph{Behavioral relevance.}
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with published LIBERO success rates yields a positive but non-significant trend (Spearman $\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$); within-suite comparisons are uniformly positive ($\rho = 1.0$ on Goal, $n = 3$; same direction on all remaining suites).
Architecture capacity differences and limited sample size preclude causal interpretation (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Synthesis.}
Training-associated effects concentrate at the readout token ($+0.069$ $R^2$ shift vs.\ $+0.015$ at image\_mean), while L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model pretraining (Phi-3-Vision: 32/32, Qwen2.5-VL: 13--14/16 before training).

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Cross-architecture evidence rests on $N = 2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions.
All experiments use LIBERO; benchmarks with richer language grounding are needed.
We analyze only causal-decoder VLAs; flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} architectures may differ.
NORA lacks 2 of 4 suite checkpoints, and the two NLP controls cover only the Llama-2 and Phi-3 backbone families.
All analyses are open-loop; closed-loop behavioral validation is left for future work (extended discussion in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Across three VLA architectures and four LIBERO suites, VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning is associated with substantial exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.15$--$0.45$), whereas VLA-to-VLA conditions show only small fluctuations ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$).

Beyond characterization, the exit-collapse diagnostic ($\Delta R^2$ threshold) and the reference-checkpoint comparison protocol offer reusable tools for evaluating instruction processing in future VLA architectures.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

Training-associated effects concentrate at the readout token ($+0.069$ $R^2$ shift vs.\ $+0.015$ at image\_mean), while L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model pretraining (Phi-3-Vision: 32/32, Qwen2.5-VL: 13--14/16 before training).
The $\Delta R^2$ threshold offers a practical diagnostic: computing per-layer action probes requires approximately one GPU-hour and no task-specific labels beyond the training data already available; a substantial drop ($\Delta R^2 > 0.10$) signals VLM-to-VLA reorganization, while a flat profile ($< 0.10$) suggests pre-existing action-decoding structure.
This pattern also motivates multi-stage pipelines---where a general-purpose action-capable checkpoint precedes task-specific fine-tuning---as a strategy that may preserve exit-layer structure.
Mid-layer probes consistently outperform exit-layer probes in architectures with pronounced collapse, motivating early-exit decoding strategies, and L1 instruction-dominant attention fractions provide a low-cost signal for verifying instruction routing after fine-tuning.
These implications are directional; validating them requires controlled training-stage experiments.

\paragraph{Behavioral relevance.}
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with published LIBERO success rates yields a positive but non-significant trend (Spearman $\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$); within-suite comparisons are uniformly positive ($\rho = 1.0$ on Goal, $n = 3$; same direction on all remaining suites).
Architecture capacity differences and limited sample size preclude causal interpretation (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Cross-architecture evidence rests on $N = 2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions; all experiments use LIBERO, and we analyze only causal-decoder VLAs (flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} architectures may differ).
NORA lacks 2 of 4 suite checkpoints, and the two NLP controls cover only the Llama-2 and Phi-3 families.
All analyses are open-loop; closed-loop behavioral validation is left for future work (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Across three VLA architectures and four LIBERO suites, VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning is associated with substantial exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.15$--$0.45$), whereas VLA-to-VLA conditions show only small fluctuations ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$).
All trained VLAs exhibit medium-to-large counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$); L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model priors; two NLP controls (both $\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) further support transition-type specificity.
Beyond characterization, the exit-collapse diagnostic ($\Delta R^2$ threshold) and the reference-checkpoint comparison protocol offer reusable tools for evaluating instruction processing in future VLA architectures.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
